summary: Melphalan is a bifunctional nitrogen-mustard alkylating agent used mainly for multiple myeloma (and ovarian cancer, and at high dose as conditioning before stem-cell transplant). It carries a BOXED WARNING: severe bone-marrow suppression (the dose-limiting toxicity) causing infection and bleeding, hypersensitivity including anaphylaxis with the IV form, and leukemogenicity/mutagenicity - it can cause secondary leukaemia and is teratogenic. It must be given under specialist supervision with frequent blood-count monitoring and dose reduction in renal impairment.
indications: Palliative treatment of multiple myeloma (where oral therapy is not appropriate - IV form)
Palliative treatment of non-resectable epithelial ovarian carcinoma (oral form)
High-dose conditioning regimen before autologous stem-cell transplantation in multiple myeloma (specialist use)

dosage.d: 16 mg/m2 as a single IV infusion over 15-20 minutes
dosage.t: Every 2 weeks x4, then every 4 weeks
dosage.n: After adequate recovery from toxicity; reduce up to 50% in renal insufficiency

dosage.d: Common regimen e.g. 0.15 mg/kg/day for 7 days, or 0.25 mg/kg/day for 4 days, repeated every 6 weeks
dosage.n: Often combined with prednisone; titrate to blood counts

dosage.d: 0.2 mg/kg/day for 5 days, repeated every 4-5 weeks

dosage.n: Only with stem-cell support and intensive monitoring

admin: Administer under the supervision of a physician experienced in cancer chemotherapy
IV: reconstitute and infuse promptly (solution is unstable) over 15-20 minutes through a fast-running infusion or central line; avoid extravasation (vesicant)
Oral: take on an empty stomach because food impairs absorption
Ensure adequate hydration with high-dose IV therapy
Have facilities to manage anaphylaxis available with IV administration; handle as a hazardous cytotoxic drug
moa: Melphalan is a bifunctional alkylating agent (a phenylalanine derivative of nitrogen mustard). It forms covalent cross-links between and within DNA strands at guanine N7 positions, preventing DNA replication and transcription and triggering cell death. Its action is not cell-cycle-phase specific, and it is particularly active against rapidly dividing cells such as myeloma plasma cells.

relative: Recent radiotherapy or other myelosuppressive chemotherapy
monitor: Complete blood count with differential and platelets (frequently)

preg: CONTRAINDICATED. Melphalan is mutagenic, can cause chromosomal damage, and is teratogenic/embryotoxic. Women of childbearing potential must avoid pregnancy and use effective contraception; men should also use contraception. It can suppress ovarian function and cause amenorrhoea.
lact: Contraindicated. It is not known whether melphalan is excreted in breast milk, but because of the potential for serious harm to the infant, breastfeeding must be discontinued during treatment.
renal: Renal impairment increases exposure and myelosuppression. For IV melphalan, consider reducing the dose by up to 50% in patients with renal insufficiency (e.g. BUN >= 30 mg/dL) and monitor blood counts closely. Adequate hydration is important with high-dose therapy.
hepatic: There are limited data in hepatic impairment; use with caution and monitor. No specific dose-adjustment scheme is established.

major: Nalidixic acid plus high-dose IV melphalan (fatal haemorrhagic necrotising enterocolitis reported in children)
Other myelosuppressive agents and radiotherapy (additive marrow suppression)
Live vaccines (risk of disseminated infection - avoid)
moderate: Cyclosporine (increased risk of renal toxicity with high-dose melphalan)
Cisplatin (cisplatin-induced renal impairment can raise melphalan exposure)
minor: Concomitant ondansetron and supportive agents - generally compatible
interactions.food: Food significantly reduces and varies oral absorption - take the oral form on an empty stomach
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction, but avoid agents that add to GI/hepatic burden
interactions.diagnostics: Causes cytopenias on blood counts; may elevate uric acid (tumour lysis); can raise liver enzymes

common: Bone marrow suppression - leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, anaemia
serious: Severe myelosuppression with neutropenic sepsis and bleeding
Secondary malignancy - acute myeloid leukaemia / myelodysplasia

monitoring: Complete blood count with differential and platelets before and frequently during therapy (and at the expected nadir)
Signs of infection, bleeding and hypersensitivity
counsel: This is a strong chemotherapy drug given under specialist care - keep all blood-test and treatment appointments
Report fever, sore throat, unusual bruising or bleeding, or signs of infection immediately
Use effective contraception during and after treatment (men and women) - it can harm a baby and affect fertility
Take oral melphalan on an empty stomach
Avoid live vaccines and tell your team about all other medicines
pk: Cytotoxic effect over days; haematologic nadir typically around 2-3 weeks
IV gives immediate peak plasma levels; oral absorption is variable and incomplete
Marrow effects persist for weeks; counts recover before the next dose
Oral tablets: refrigerate 2-8 C, protect from light; IV vials per label, reconstitute immediately before use and use promptly (solution unstable)
pearls: BOXED WARNING: severe myelosuppression, hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis (IV), and leukemogenic/mutagenic potential
Oral absorption is erratic and reduced by food - give on an empty stomach and titrate to blood counts
Reduce the IV dose in renal impairment; the kidney influences clearance and toxicity
Secondary acute leukaemia/MDS is a recognised long-term risk of alkylating-agent therapy
High-dose IV melphalan is a backbone of autologous stem-cell transplant conditioning in myeloma - requires stem-cell rescue
missed: Melphalan is given in supervised cycles. If an oral dose is missed, contact the oncology team rather than doubling up - they will advise on timing. Missed or delayed IV doses are rescheduled by the treating team based on blood counts and recovery.
overdose: Overdose causes severe, potentially fatal bone-marrow suppression (profound neutropenia and thrombocytopenia), severe mucositis, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. There is no specific antidote - management is intensive supportive care including antibiotics for neutropenic sepsis, blood-product support, growth factors, and consideration of haematopoietic stem-cell support after very high exposures. Maintain hydration and monitor counts until recovery.
